title: Tonglen
hookLine: sending and taking: breathe in another's pain, breathe out relief

cards: Breathe in calm. Breathe out tension. It's the usual line in a yoga class or a stress app: take in the good, push out the bad.
It makes a kind of sense; it's how people treat anything that hurts. Tonglen turns it exactly around. Breathe in someone else's pain.
Breathe out relief, toward them. It sounds backward, maybe even a little risky. Tibetan teachers have long taught it as a practice of compassion.

teach.b: Tonglen is two Tibetan words. Tong: sending, giving away. Len: taking, receiving.

It belongs to the mind-training teachings, tomorrow's subject, and one of their short sayings puts it simply: practice sending and taking in turn, and let the two ride the breath. Here's how teachers usually describe it.
As you breathe in, you picture taking in someone's suffering, often imagined as dark, heavy smoke. As you breathe out, you send them relief: light, coolness, space, whatever would help.
Teachers often suggest starting where it's easiest. First your own pain, just as it is.
Then someone you love who's hurting. Then a stranger who feels the same thing. Then everyone who feels it tonight.
Why would anyone breathe in pain?
Because, the teachers say, the habit of shoving pain away and grabbing comfort is exactly what keeps the heart small and scared.
Tonglen reverses the habit, and over time, they say, pain becomes less frightening, not more. Does it take the pain away from the other person? Teachers answer in different ways.

Some say its main work is on the practitioner's own heart; others hold that it can truly benefit the person held in mind. It's karuna, compassion, one of the four rooms from the start of this camp, given a rhythm.
And there's a gentle rule. If it overwhelms you, go back to your own pain, or simply rest. Nobody is asked to carry the whole world in one breath.

how: Tibetan Buddhists practice tonglen as part of mind training, usually beginning with their own suffering and widening to others, breathing in suffering and breathing out relief; it's also practiced at the bedside of the sick and dying.

games.q: you try tonglen for a friend who's grieving, and it starts to feel like too much. what do teachers usually advise?
o: keep going until it stops hurting.
come back to your own pain or simply rest.
switch to breathing in calm instead.
games.why: teachers say to start where it's easy and never force it; nobody is asked to carry the whole world in one breath.

practice: Start with something you feel right now, a tiredness or a worry: breathe it in as if making room for it, not fighting it, and breathe out ease toward yourself.

After a few breaths, think of one person who is struggling, breathe in their heaviness, and breathe out something that might help them. If it ever feels like too much, go back to your own breath and rest.
